name: Adam Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't go with any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a farm worker at Ferncombe, which the Pryce family runs: three hundred outdoor sows, sixty acres of potatoes and some wheat. My day starts with the pig rounds on the quad bike, checking the arks, the water lines and the electric fence. Afternoons it's whatever Gwen Pryce needs, grading potatoes in the store or helping the contractor at harvest. I like being outside after years indoors, and I don't like mud in my boots from October to March.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Twelve years in a call centre for a broadband company, answering angry people about their router. I saw the chatbots coming for that job and got out two years ago, which felt clever until I saw farm wages. I'm still learning, honestly, and I ask an AI app about everything, from sow body condition to blight warnings. My partner Lucie is a teaching assistant, we've got Noah, who's eleven, and Elsie, who's eight, and a mortgage on an old council house in Kelby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not shocked, because I use these tools every day and they make mistakes all the time. I'd tell the lads in the potato store it's a good helper, not a boss. Online I'd probably post a long thread about who got rich off the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the money worries stay exactly where they are. I'm on the lowest rate at Ferncombe, and the mortgage fixed rate ends next spring. My job's safe enough, because Gwen needs hands for three hundred sows whether AI is hype or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the app to learn the pigs faster, because the quicker I'm good, the quicker I can ask for a raise. I'd ask Gwen about the stockperson certificate, the one that puts me on the next pay band. And I'd ring the bank in January before the fixed rate runs out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit restless, because I left one job and the new one pays less. I'd feel like I bet right but haven't been paid yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do you lean on the AI app day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably ten times a day. I'll take a photo of a sow's skin and ask what it is, then I check with Gwen anyway. My phone taught me more about pigs in two years than I'd have learned on my own in five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when the fixed rate ends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The payment goes up about a hundred and forty a month, Lucie worked it out. We'd drop the streaming, the takeaway Friday, and probably Noah's swimming club. I'd hate cutting the swimming most.

say: I'd say AI is a **good helper**, not a boss, and makes plenty of mistakes.
I'd post about **who got rich** off the hype.
think: I think my **job is safe**, because three hundred sows still need hands.
I think the real worry is the **fixed rate ending** next spring.
do: Keep using the **AI app** daily to learn the pigs faster.
Ask Gwen about the **stockperson certificate** for the next pay band.
Ring the bank in **January** before the fixed rate ends.
feel: He feels **restless**, like he bet right on farming but hasn't been **paid yet**.
S0.quote: My phone taught me more about pigs in two years than I'd have learned on my own in five.
fieldNote: He left a **call centre** to escape chatbots, so he reads AI news more closely than most farmhands.
He uses AI **ten times a day** but still checks with Gwen, a careful habit.
His real pressure is a **£140 mortgage jump**, which would cost Noah's swimming club.

steps.text: Use the AI app every day to learn sow health
Ask Gwen to put me forward for the stockperson certificate
Drop streaming and Friday takeaways when the mortgage rises

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the call centre story again, and I lived it. I'd tell people the farm is safer for now, but the office side of farming is changing fast. Online I'd say the companies saving money should pay for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's my chance. Gwen does the ordering, the pig records and the potato contracts at night after tea, and she hates it. If I'm the farmhand who can set up the software, Gwen (his boss) keeps me on even when the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to set up the farm's feed ordering and record apps over the winter, for free at first. I'd watch every video on the pig-shed robots, so when Gwen asks I've got answers. I'd also tell Lucie to learn the marking software at school before it learns her job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly, with a bit of guilt. I know it's bad news for loads of people, and I'm half looking forward to it. That doesn't sit right with my politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say it's bad news for others but good for you. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't, really. I think the tools should help workers, not replace them, and I'd vote that way. But I've got a mortgage, so I'll make myself useful while I'm waiting for the world to get fairer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Lucie's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching assistants do a lot of the reading practice and marking, and that's exactly the thinking stuff this takes. Lucie's worried about the school budget already. If her hours go, we're in trouble, because I'm on the lowest band.

say: I'd say this is the **call centre story** again, and I lived it.
I'd say companies saving money should **pay for retraining**.
think: I think it's **my chance**, because Gwen hates the **night paperwork**.
I think **Lucie's school hours** are more at risk than my farm job.
do: Set up the farm's **feed ordering and records** apps over winter.
Study the **pig-shed robots** so I have answers when Gwen asks.
Push Lucie to learn the **marking software** early.
feel: He feels **excited** with some **guilt**, because his gain is other people's loss.
S1.quote: If I'm the farmhand who can set up the software, Gwen (his boss) keeps me on even when the robots come.
fieldNote: He sees Steady Disruption as an **opening**, since the farm's paperwork is the part he can take over.
He names the clash between his **politics and self-interest** and doesn't resolve it.
The household risk sits with **Lucie's thinking-heavy work** as a teaching assistant.

steps.text: Set up Ferncombe's feed ordering and pig records apps
Watch training videos on pig-shed robots
Help Lucie learn the school's marking software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a proper safety net, paid for by whoever owns the robots. I'd say it loud, at the pub and online. I'd also say farmers who adapt fast will be fine, which is half true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 the AI does Gwen's planning, and that's fine for me. In 2031 a robot does the pig rounds and the grading, and Ferncombe needs maybe one person to keep the machines running. I'd have three years to make myself the one person Gwen (his boss) keeps, and so would every other farmhand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd do the pig robot maintenance course online, in the evenings. I'd ask Gwen if I can run the trial when the first robot comes, even unpaid. I'd also start a weekend thing setting up farm apps for older farmers round Kelby, fifty quid a visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but awake. I've done this jump before. The difference is I had a bit of savings when I left the call centre, and now I've got none.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Gwen picks someone else as the robot person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go and be the robot person on someone else's farm, if there are any left hiring. That's the bit that frightens me, because there are only four farms like Ferncombe within a half-hour drive. We might have to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving mean for the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noah would be starting secondary school, so it would be the worst year to pull him out. Elsie would probably cope. Lucie would say no, and Lucie would probably be right.

say: I'd call for a **safety net** paid for by **robot owners**.
I'd say farmers who **adapt fast** will be fine, which is half true.
think: I think by 2031 Ferncombe needs maybe **one person** to run the machines.
I think I have **three years** to become that one person.
do: Take the **pig robot maintenance** course online in the evenings.
Ask Gwen to let me **run the robot trial**, even unpaid.
Start a **weekend service** setting up farm apps for £50 a visit.
feel: He feels **anxious but awake**, because he's made a jump before.
He knows he jumped last time **with savings**, and now has none.
S2.quote: I'd have three years to make myself the one person Gwen (his boss) keeps, and so would every other farmhand.
fieldNote: He reads the **three-year gap** as a race to be the last farmhand kept.
His fallback is moving, but **only four similar farms** lie within half an hour.
His adaptability is real, but **no savings** limits how far he can jump.

steps.text: Take the online pig robot maintenance course in the evenings
Ask Gwen to let me run the first robot trial
Set up farm apps for older farmers at £50 a visit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if we start now, so let's start. I'd talk it up at the pig producers' group meeting. Online I'd share how-tos, because a lot of farmers my age don't know where to begin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the same race as the two-year one, but with a better start. By 2034 I could have the robot course done and two years running Ferncombe's machines. Five years turns me from the new lad into the lad who knows the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the maintenance course in year one and a short electrics course in year two. I'd build up the farm app side business slowly, maybe one visit a week. I'd put every app fee into savings so we finally get two months' cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with the usual money knot. I can actually picture it working. I'd still check the bank app every Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Ferncombe would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dariusz, who does the potato grading and doesn't speak much English. Dariusz is the best grader there, but a camera grader would do it faster. I'd want Gwen to put Dariusz on the robot course with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change how you vote or organise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd vote the same way, for whoever wants workers to share what the robots save. I might join the farmworkers' union too, which I haven't yet. Being the robot person doesn't stop me wanting it fair.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to get ready** if we start now.
I'd share **how-tos** at the pig producers' group and online.
think: I think five years turns me into **the lad who knows** the robots.
I think the race is the same, but with a **better start**.
do: Do the **robot maintenance course** in year one and electrics in year two.
Grow the **farm app side business** to one visit a week.
Put every app fee into savings to reach **two months' cushion**.
feel: He feels **hopeful**, with his usual **money knot**.
S3.quote: Five years turns me from the new lad into the lad who knows the robots.
fieldNote: Five years gives him time to **build a cushion** and a skill, which two years didn't.
He worries about **Dariusz the grader**, whose job a camera could take.
He'd join the **union** even while planning to be the robot person.

steps.text: Finish the robot maintenance course, then a short electrics course
Grow the farm app setup business to one visit a week
Save every app fee until we have two months' cushion
Join the farmworkers' union this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and the farms that waste it deserve what they get. That sounds harsh, so I'd say it nicer at the pub. Online I'd push for free robot training at the agricultural college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and three more for the robots puts me at fifty-six with the kids grown. Ten years is enough time for a call-centre man to become a robot engineer, and I'd bet my mortgage on it. The savings are still thin, but time is the thing I was short of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a proper part-time diploma in agricultural engineering over three years. I'd use AI for Ferncombe's records right away, so Gwen trusts me with the systems. I'd talk to Lucie about her retraining too, maybe as a school tech assistant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. It's the first one that feels like a plan instead of a scramble. I'd still worry about the money, but less about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd bet your mortgage on it. Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not literally, Lucie would kill me. I mean I'd spend the evenings and the weekends on it. That's what I've got instead of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the robots get owned by three big companies and farms like Ferncombe get bought out. Then it doesn't matter what I learn. That's a politics problem, not a farm one.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty**, and farms that waste it pay for it.
I'd push for **free robot training** at the agricultural college.
think: I think ten years is enough to become a **robot engineer**.
I think the real risk is **big companies buying out** farms like Ferncombe.
do: Start a **part-time diploma** in agricultural engineering over three years.
Use AI for Ferncombe's **records** so Gwen trusts me with systems.
Help Lucie plan a move to **school tech assistant**.
feel: He feels **pretty good**, because this one is a **plan**, not a scramble.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough time for a call-centre man to become a robot engineer, and I'd bet my mortgage on it.
fieldNote: With ten years he expects to **come out ahead**, so the worry shifts from his job to ownership.
He offers **evenings and weekends** in place of money he doesn't have.
His deepest fear is **corporate buyouts**, which he calls a politics problem.

steps.text: Start a part-time agricultural engineering diploma
Use AI to run Ferncombe's pig and potato records
Help Lucie plan a move to school tech assistant

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because three years isn't enough to build anything with no savings. What would help is free robot courses at the college and a rule that farms like Ferncombe share some of what the robots save. I can learn anything, but learning doesn't pay the mortgage while I'm doing it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I regret leaving the call centre. I don't, even on the muddy days. I'd do it again, and I'd do the next jump too.

headlineQuote: I can learn anything, but learning doesn't pay the mortgage while I'm doing it.
portrait: Adam left a **call centre** job two years ago and is still learning pigs and potatoes at Ferncombe.
He uses **AI daily** to learn faster and sees farm software as his way to stay needed.
His partner Lucie's **teaching assistant** hours and a rising mortgage are the household's weak points.
He moves from **uneasy** to anxious as robots near, but feels he can win the race to be kept.
He leans left and fears **big companies owning** the robots more than the robots themselves.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three years with no savings is too short to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: Free **robot courses** at the college and a rule that farms **share** the savings.
